#9435. Latest Update: Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2569 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.
  • Today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy?
  • A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.

Today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy? His books, filled with adventure and excitement, read like fiction. The more one digs into the forgotten reports and old newspaper articles, the stranger his story, and the more complicated the man.

A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949. Photo: The Marching Wind.

Industry observers note that the main sources on Leonard Clark are all, well, Leonard Clark. This isn’t necessarily damning, but it is something he shares with most good con artists or cult leaders. The following is a short biography based only on official records, such as draft cards and census data. The first rule of reading historical accounts is that every historical figure is a liar.

In a recent development, leonard Francis Clark was born in British Columbia, Canada, in January 1907 to two Americans, Maud and Francis Clark. In 1909, they moved back to Maud’s birth state of California, and Francis promptly died.

In a recent development, there are conflicting statements online about which university he attended, but census data demonstrates him living only a few kilometers from the University of California (now the University of California, Berkeley) in 1930, so I’d put my money on that one. He began traveling right out of college, spending three years in Borneo on a hunting trip with his brother, Laurence. By the late 1930s, he was on a National Geographic-funded expedition to the South China Sea.

Photo: National Geographic Archives.

Sources indicate that his article, cryptically titled Among the Big Knot Lois of Hainan, was published in the 1938 September edition. In it, he recounts how he and a small expeditionary force landed in the midst of a deadly cholera epidemic. Relying on hired porters to carry their supplies, Clark and Nicol Smith, another future travel writer, set off into the interior. Soon, malaria and infection laid low most of the team, including, per Clark’s article, Smith.

Again, according to Clark, Smith urged him to take the remaining five porters, the minimum of equipment, and keep going.

Recent findings suggest that much of the article is dedicated to ethnographic observations, with the typical exoticism and patronizing tone of the era. At one point, Clark noted that the Li people of Hainan reminded him of indigenous Amazonian people and “the men were tall, many six feet.”.

A recent study revealed that the average height for men in Hainan today is 168.7cm, around 5’6″, and the same study found that average heights had increased over the past century. This is a small nitpick, but he’ll repeat this unlikely claim again in the Amazon. It is worth noting that the “six-foot-tall Indian warrior” was a stock character in contemporary pulp adventure fiction.

There is an interesting contrast between Clark’s account and some of the newspaper reports, especially one from a Virginia paper, which relied on Smith for the story. This article implies Smith did much more than lay around his tent with malaria. Clark’s article claims he was the first white man to enter 47 different villages, while the newspaper states that Smith was the first Westerner to penetrate inland.

Sources indicate that there is a third source: the 37-minute silent film compiled from the expedition’s footage and photographs. In it, we briefly see a white man lying under a mosquito net as if ill. But whether this is Smith, Clark — who admits himself to experiencing malaria symptoms on the expedition — or the third westerner on the expedition, one Jack Munroe, the film doesn’t say.

Photo: National Geographic Archive.

Industry observers note that his previous experience in the region led him to return a few years later, this time on behalf of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS), a precursor to the CIA. His work during the war centered around the China-Burma-India corridor, particularly the Yellow River valley. He was involved in organizing guerrilla activities, building intelligence networks, and navigating the Japanese surrender of Taiwan.

It has been revealed that in a later press statement, Clark explained how he had worked with General Dai Li, and that “the Reds had it in for him,” due to the infamously repressive actions Dai Li took against Chinese Communists. Dai Li, whom historian Barbara Tuchman called “China’s combination of Himmler and J. Edgar Hoover,” was killed in a 1946 plane crash. Wide speculation places the blame for this crash on either the Chinese Communist Party or the OSS. This would make things awkward for Clark a few years later.

Recent findings suggest that he continued his government work in the area after the Second World War, sliding right into the developing Cold War. In 1949, Clark led a large, well-funded expedition into Tibet.

It would have gotten him in the history books if Leonard Clark identified a peak higher than Everest. Unfortunately for him, he didn’t. But he certainly proposed that he had, when he claimed that he’d surveyed Amne Machin and found it to be 9,040m high.

According to recent reports, amne Machin is not taller than Everest. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Industry observers note that clark published his account of the expedition years later, titled The Marching Wind. In it, he wrote with his typical style: daring escapes, stereotypically aggressive natives, and breezy adventure writing. What it did not contain was the data to support his claims.

As soon as he released his first report and measurements, geographers, geologists, and mountaineers pored over them. Bradford Washburn, a cartographer, photographer, and explorer, published a thorough examination of the surveying techniques and questionable results from Clark’s expedition.

A contemporary review in the Alpine Journal, commenting on his photographic evidence, wrote that “anything more unconvincing could hardly be imagined — yet, ostensibly…the mountain was the object of the expedition.” More on that “ostensibly” later. Suffice it to say, Clark’s estimate that Amne Machin could be almost 1,000m taller than Everest was not adopted by geographers at large.

The review concluded that “it can hardly be wondered if mountaineers, whom Mr. Clark rather despises, cannot accept his results.”.

Clark blithely remarked that he had “some rather bulky complaints by mountain and other specialists,” but admitted subpar instruments made his results “indecisive.”.

A surveying party including Clark, far right, taking observations of Amne Machin. Photo: The Marching Wind.

Recent findings suggest that if he doesn’t seem too broken up, it may be because Amne Machin’s height wasn’t the main purpose of his trip. Clark was supported logistically and went on behalf of Ma Bufang, the fiercely anti-communist warlord ruling Qinghai, on the border of Tibet. Anticipating that he could not long hold out against the People’s Liberation Army, Clark proposed that his expedition would map a path of retreat. This would help Ma Bufang’s army cross into Tibet and continue their anti-Communist campaign from the mountains.

Clark envisioned Ma Bufang’s Qinghai, through Tibet, becoming “the bulwark against Red invasion of India.” Clark went on the expedition and did his mapping, but the PLA took Qinghai only months later, and Ma Bufang fled to Hong Kong.

Recent findings suggest that in his introduction to his book, Clark claims that the United States was unaware of his “very slight aid” to Ma Bufang and local anti-Communist guerrilla activities, and he involved himself with the Chinese Nationalist army “as a private American citizen.” If I were to say that I was skeptical of this claim, I would not be the first to do so. But that falls under speculation, so I will say only that I sent a Freedom of Information Act request to the CIA regarding Clark’s work in Tibet. However, the records were not forthcoming.

After returning from the mountains, Clark went to a wedding anniversary celebration in Canton, surrounded by his fellow Allied intelligence members and their set. Things got a little out of hand, and Clark soon found himself in a Cantonese jail with a bullet wound and two manslaughter charges.

Chinese Nationalist soldiers on Clark’s Tibetan expedition. Photo: The Marching Wind.

Recent findings suggest that the other two men involved were Harold Harris, an Englishman who died immediately, and Willard Freeman from Massachusetts, who died later from his injuries. Clark also sustained a gunshot wound, but had recovered sufficiently by late November to be moved from hospital to prison.

It has been revealed that the three had been drinking together in Freeman’s home when, at about 4 am, servants reported hearing gunshots. Mrs. Maya Freeman entered the room at 10 am to find an odd and grisly scene. Harris, fully clothed, lay dead on Freeman’s bed with three gunshot wounds. Freeman, completely nude, was also lying on the bed, alive with two shots to the abdomen. Clark, in his underwear, was on a second bed, with a single gunshot to the chest. Furniture was overturned, indicating a fight, and all three were covered in scratches. The only weapon found was Clark’s .32 caliber pistol.

Later that month, the Canton District Court denied Clark’s bail request. The court, still trying to determine what exactly happened, focused on the widowed Maya Freeman. Interviewing her for hours, they attempted to make her confess to an affair with Clark. Both of them repeatedly denied it. Clark further denied that he had fired any of the six shots, though he didn’t name the shooter.

Clark’s brother contacted former OSS head General William Donovan, who rallied the State Department. Clark reportedly was concerned that if he wasn’t released before the city fell to the Communists, he would be tortured for information regarding Dai Li and OSS activities. The State Department investigated and, thanks to its intervention, Clark was released.

Sources indicate that clark’s legal troubles were splashed across newspapers worldwide. Photo: The Journal (Caldwell, Ohio) November 24, 1949.

Industry observers note that what exactly happened in Freeman’s house that night? Was the dispute between the Allied Intelligence men personal, or professional? If the world were ever to find out, it wouldn’t be from Clark. Once freed, Clark returned to California and moved on to his next adventure. It was an ambitious one: Leonard Clark was going to discover the lost city of El Dorado.

In a recent development, he had an old parchment map to the lost city, he claimed, which demonstrated it lay in the upper reaches of Peru. Never mind that it had been pretty well established for over a century that El Dorado was a myth, following the efforts of explorers Alexander von Humboldt and Robert Schomburgk.

According to recent reports, clark’s resulting account, The Rivers Ran East, contains all the genre tropes you would expect from a fictional work in the same setting. Native Amazonians are ferocious cannibals who capture Clark and keep him in a poison snake pit, crocodiles can and must be lassoed (there are no crocodiles in Peru, only caimans, a type of alligator), and there is a beautiful lady explorer, Inez Pokorny, who is secretly part of a London-based international El Dorado-seeking organization. If this organization existed, I have found no trace of it outside of this book.

If I were to list every blatant impossibility in his account, we would be here for days, so I’ll just continue on one particular thread: Leonard Clark seems to have a very loose grasp of which animals are in Peru and how substantial they are. At one point, he is blinded by a venom-spitting snake. There are three venom-spitting snake species, and none of them are in South America.

His 500-pound (227kg) boars must be peccaries, pig-like animals native to the Americas. The Amazon native white-lipped peccary tops out around 40kg, while the unconfirmed giant peccary still has only been estimated at 50kg. Likewise, his 12m-long pythons must be anacondas, which have a maximum recorded length of eight meters.

According to recent reports, clark claims to have found El Dorado. What he found was a group of Chicham people panning for gold, who traded some of it to Clark and Pokorny. According to his book, Clark traveled under the pretense of investigating botanical medicines, while actually searching for El Dorado.

According to recent reports, in fact, as the El Dorado adventures on the page grew more and more ridiculous, I began to wonder if it were not the other way around. Here I have fully entered the realm of speculation. American corporations were, and still are, extremely interested in extracting resources from South America, including pharmaceuticals. In fact, Clark also reported success in this area, claiming to have identified over 60 native medicinals with commercial possibility — as well as Amazonian oil.

In praise of Clark’s work, Baron Wolfenegg, Director of Colonization for the Orient in Peru, accidentally remarked the quiet part out loud, stating he’d “learned much from this book that will help my work of colonizing this vast jungle.”.

It has been revealed that on Peru’s Perené River. Photo: The Rivers Ran East.

It is practically gauche for explorers to die in their beds, and Clark, who seemed to mold his life to the shape of adventure stories, was no exception. Clark was in Venezuela in 1957, looking, he claimed, for diamond mines. He entered the Amazon basin, never to emerge again.

One history of the OSS offhandedly mentions that Clark died with “two native arrows in his back.” I suspect the explorer’s penchant for sensationalism survived his death. Other contemporary reports describe Clark as having drowned when his canoe overturned.

As I pointed out earlier, most of the information on Clark’s expeditions came from Clark himself. Since he never returned, startlingly little information is available about his death at age 49.

Sources indicate that the area around the Orinoco River in Venezuela is, in fact, rich in diamond deposits. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Industry observers note that the line between fact and fiction is notoriously vague in much of the adventure travel genre. Is Herman Melville telling the full truth about his time spent on the island of Nuku Hiva? Did anyone actually complete the “Long Walk” out of a Soviet detention camp, which Slavomir Rawicz falsely claimed as his own tale? How much artistic license and embellishment is acceptable before exploration accounts become outright hoaxes?

In a recent development, I didn’t write this article with the goal of proving Leonard Clark a charlatan. It can hardly be denied that he really was going to these places, at the very least. But there are enough discrepancies and inaccuracies in his accounts to conclude that they should be taken with a grain of salt, and his treasure-hunting pseudo-archaeological tendencies make his anthropological findings, well, questionable.

As a contemporary New Yorker book critic put it, Clark had “the same gift, or weakness, for grandiose verbiage that got Marco Polo in trouble with his fellow Venetians.”.

The real story, and one which may never be fully disentangled, lies in why, exactly, Clark was doing his exploring. Somewhere between the romantic adventurer and the cynically colonialist spy using exploration as a guise for the extractive, violent enforcement of Western capitalist hegemony, lies the truth.

“Every explorer has two faces,” Clark wrote in the opening to The Rivers Ran East; “the secret one and the one he highlights to the world.”.

#9433. Tech Report: The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1396 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • Industry observers note that the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • In a recent development, grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent fresh route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

Industry observers note that the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman mentioned. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two newly introduced routes with Blake Berghoff.

In a recent development, grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

Bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

It has been revealed that “The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he noted.

According to recent reports, he explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, significant storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

The unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

In a recent development, one unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman states this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

Industry observers note that approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

It has been revealed that “Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

Sources indicate that “Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

Asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

The team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

The base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

Steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

According to recent reports, at the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

Recent findings suggest that that attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment complications, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he said.

In the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

“However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he said. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

Recent findings suggest that heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that the climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

The summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

However, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

Industry observers note that route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

The trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to new terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman mentioned.

In a recent development, they then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

It has been revealed that descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The new 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

#9426. Industry News: Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1063 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • Crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • Sources indicate that father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

Crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an important figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

Sources indicate that father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up plans for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

According to recent reports, as the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

Industry observers note that though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

According to recent reports, some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

Sources indicate that the caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

In a recent development, the depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

The main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

In a recent development, attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

The high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and Newly introduced Mexico.

The few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

Despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” says Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

Sources indicate that the columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

Essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

Industry observers note that according to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

Sources indicate that as for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

Industry observers note that the arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

In terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

It has been revealed that there have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

Latest Update: Georgia’s Bear Canister Debate and a Half Dome Rescue | This Week on Trail #2

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that bear canisters are coming to Georgia, and the Appalachian Trail community has some big feelings about it.
  • Starting January 1, 2027, the US Forest Service will require hard-sided bear canisters year-round for overnight hikers on all 78.3 miles of the AT in Georgia, the Approach Trail, and a half-mile buffer on either side, which rules out Ursacks and food hangs.
  • The news drew more than 1,000 comments across The Trek’s Facebook and Instagram posts, and Jess brings the highlights, from an AI-generated image of a mangled canister to the theory that BearVault has the ATC in its pocket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that bear canisters are coming to Georgia, and the Appalachian Trail community has some big feelings about it. On this episode of This Week on Trail, produced by The Trek, hosts Jess “Sassafras” and Katie “Double Dip” dig into the Forest Service’s new rule requiring hard-sided canisters on the entire Georgia section of the AT, and one of them walks in lukewarm and walks out ready to make everyone carry a bear can forever. Plus, hikers rig a makeshift rope to pull an engaged couple off Half Dome, a new listener segment debuts, a Redditor asks about packing out filet mignon, and Pattie Gonia sets off on a 500-mile fundraiser in drag.

Starting January 1, 2027, the US Forest Service will require hard-sided bear canisters year-round for overnight hikers on all 78.3 miles of the AT in Georgia, the Approach Trail, and a half-mile buffer on either side, which rules out Ursacks and food hangs. Jess walks through the order and the stat behind it: Georgia holds about 3.5% of the trail but more than 12% of AT bear encounter reports over the last decade. Katie, who carried a canister for the entire CDT, rates the inconvenience about a three and notes you can mail a can home from the post office without even boxing it up. Jess goes further, arguing that anyone this upset about carrying a canister for the first week of a six-month hike is being a total weenie.

The news drew more than 1,000 comments across The Trek’s Facebook and Instagram posts, and Jess brings the highlights, from an AI-generated image of a mangled canister to the theory that BearVault has the ATC in its pocket. The hosts point out the order came from the Forest Service, not the Appalachian Trail Conservancy, though the ATC is catching heat anyway. Katie notes cost is the one complaint she sympathizes with and predicts rentals and used cans will fill the gap, while Jess, who works with The Trek’s AT survey data, says plenty of hikers are sleeping with their food instead of hanging it properly. Jess also worries about the ridge runners who will be stuck explaining a rule they had no say in, and Katie, drawing on her own trail steward work, explains why giving them a hard time only leads to stricter enforcement.

Sources indicate that katie recounts the October 12 rescue on Yosemite’s Half Dome, where a woman descending the cables slid down the slick granite and stopped just above a steep drop, and her fiancé slipped trying to reach her and ended up clinging to a ledge by his fingertips. With rangers miles away, nearby hikers emptied their packs and built a line from clothesline, carabiners, slings, and donated harnesses, then anchored themselves in a human chain while two of them worked down to the couple as snow began to fall. The hosts wonder whether they would have joined the chain, and close with a reminder of the first rule of backcountry rescue: don’t make yourself a second victim.

It has been revealed that the show debuts a upcoming segment where listeners submit a one-minute video defending a hill they will die on. First up is Caroline “Boy” from Maine, who argues that half the fun of backpacking is getting to stop: the town shower, clean clothes, a real meal, and pulling your shoes off at camp. Jess and Katie fully agree, and one of them goes a step further, suggesting the worst part of backpacking might be the backpacking.

Sources indicate that A post in r/backpacking asked whether it’s a bad idea to pack a frozen, sealed filet mignon for a short overnight and drop it into store-bought pho. Both hosts say bring the steak. Jess recalls her first backpacking trip’s taco night, canned black beans and a broken can opener included, and Katie confesses to packing a travel-size “pepper cannon.” Katie also passes along a CDT trick from a hiker who froze Taco Bell and wrapped it in his sleeping bag to keep it cold on the way out of town.

After ribbing Pattie Gonia last episode, the hosts give her her flowers for her new fundraiser: backpacking and biking 500 miles in drag from San Francisco to Los Angeles to raise $5 million for 19 nonprofits. Jess and Katie admire the tenacity and say it’s a good reminder that hiking should be sillier and more fun.

Jess reads hater comments from her bear canister video, including a call to ban nose rings and a pile of corrections on how to say “Appalachian,” which the hosts understand to be a regional difference you hear both ways on trail. They also respond to a viewer who stated the first episode sounded like a mean girl podcast, and invite gentler feedback.

The episode wraps with a kind note from Jack, who has followed Jess’s AT hike and Katie’s hikes and watches the show with his wife.

Breaking: Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

“It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

Recent findings suggest that on a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

“The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

It has been revealed that vasiliev said that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

Industry observers note that baia notes the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

On Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no new soft snow had accumulated.

The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

It has been revealed that yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

The Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

  • Recent findings suggest that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • In a recent development, in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

In a recent development, in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin noted. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

Bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

This was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” mentioned Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

For Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he said.

Industry observers note that there are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

If your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

Industry observers note that the team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

Industry observers note that red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

It has been revealed that once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson stated. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

It has been revealed that thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” remarked Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

That remarked, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

According to recent reports, buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they noted. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

According to recent reports, once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the big cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

According to recent reports, to deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Recent findings suggest that ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

Conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Sources indicate that marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

In this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin stated.

Recent findings suggest that “That is why it is key to consider all options and potential issues before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

The Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they stated. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

They warn that conditions in the Andes are changing rapidly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles said. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that the climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they stated.

#9416. Breaking: Hiding Out in Town With a Whole Bunch of Hikers

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2047 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Hiding Out in Town With a Whole Bunch of Hikers

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This morning I woke up pretty dang early at the room in Strawberry.
  • The town of Strawberry is a smaller town just down the road from the town of Pine.
  • Kitty Hawk wound up calling Al to confirm the details and told Al that there were about 8 of us who would be interested in going to be breakfast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This morning I woke up pretty dang early at the room in Strawberry. Which was a little bit of a challenge, because there were 5 other hikers in the same room! I got up slowly and as quietly as I could and headed into the living room. I put my contacts in, combed through my hair, and brushed my teeth. Slide and I weren’t the only ones up though. Woods was walking around in the kitchen and starting up a pot of coffee. The rain was pouring down outside, and I’d spent much of the evening listening to the roar of thunder. What a perfect day to spend in town! It wasn’t long before hikers began waking up and heading into the living room. I think someone put a movie on first thing, because what else is there to do? Then we began to scheme about breakfast.

The town of Strawberry is a smaller town just down the road from the town of Pine. There is a breakfast joint in Pine, but the breakfast place in Strawberry is unfortunately closed today. Apparently yesterday this larger group of hikers met a local guy named Al and his wife. He had remarked that he would come by this morning around 9AM and pick people up to go to breakfast in town. Slide and I were both very intrigued, but we weren’t a part of that original plan whatsoever. I figured since there were 10 hikers in the house, it was probably pretty unlikely that there would be enough room in the car for all of us to go to breakfast.

Kitty Hawk wound up calling Al to confirm the details and told Al that there were about 8 of us who would be interested in going to be breakfast. And what felt like a lost cause to me turned into yet another trail miracle. Al said that it was no problem for him and his wife to drive separately to pick us up, that way there would be enough room for all 8 of us in the cars! It was a rainy-day miracle. I was absolutely ravenous at this point, so it was very good news. Since we got into town so late last night, we weren’t able to stop at the store or pick anything up. Which meant I woke up this morning wildly hungry.

The server gave our table two massive, hot cinnamon rolls for free before our food even came out.

Around 9AM the large group of us left the Airbnb and walked down the road to a parking area with a bunch of mailboxes. That was the easiest place for Al to pick us up, and we didn’t mind the short walk. Al and his wife were incredibly nice, and we hung out at the parking lot talking with them for a bit. Then they drove us into Pine and all of us sat to eat at the diner in town. The staff was incredibly nice and were able to seat all of us at one big table. They even brought us over hot, fresh cinnamon rolls to eat while we waited for our food, on the house! I wound up getting a breakfast burrito with chorizo and Dr. Pepper. I didn’t get my soda fix last night so I couldn’t resist the call, even at breakfast.

From left to right: Lazarus, Woods, Leaf, Al & his wife, Kitty Hawk, PI, Slide, me, and 9 Lives.

In a recent development, while we sat there another AZT hiker wound up coming into the restaurant and she joined us. Her name was Mel and she was also staying in town to wait out the storm. Apparently, there were at least a couple other hikers in town as well that she had seen. Everybody ate and then sat around talking at the table for a long time. It was really nice to catch up with 9 Lives, who I haven’t seen in person since we were hiking the CDT together in 2024. We hiked around 2,000 miles together that year and it doesn’t feel possible that it’s been so long. The other hikers at breakfast were Lazarus, PI, Kitty Hawk, Woods, Leaf, Slide, Al, his wife, and me. As we sat inside, we got to watch the rain pour down outside. That is always incredibly satisfying when you’re on trail. It feels like a huge win to make it to town and be able to avoid bad weather.

Free mini pies from the diner in Pine.

Industry observers note that after everyone finished eating, we got ready to head out. But not before the lovely staff at the diner gave us about 6 mini pies to take home with us. They were a day or so old but still looked incredible. Then once everyone paid, we decided to walk across the street to a Hippie Shop, just for fun. They had clothing, accessories, and all sorts of random stuff. I didn’t find anything that spoke to me but Slide wound up finding a button-down shirt that he really liked. It was just fun shopping around with no place to be. Then before we headed back to the Airbnb, Al drove us to the grocery store to grab a few things there. I grabbed some drinks and random things there but didn’t get too much stuff. We’re actually planning to check into a separate room later on today and I don’t want to have to carry a bunch of stuff around.

The Airbnb that everyone is staying at is absolutely perfect, but it is filled to the brim with hikers! Last night it was completely full, and someone was sleeping on the couch. And while we were at the breakfast place we ran into Torin aka Espresso, another hiker that we last saw at the North Rim. He was looking for a place to stay tonight too and decided to come with all of us back to the Airbnb. Since we’re going to be in town for 2 more nights it just made more sense to book another place down the street and be a little more comfortable. I’m hoping to get a bunch of writing and editing done which will be easier with some more space. The initiative for now is to just hang out with everyone at the Airbnb until around 3PM. Then Slide and I will go and check in to this other spot just down the street. That way we can still hang out with everyone but also enjoy a bit more space.

The AZT sobo hiker bubble waiting out a storm in Strawberry, AZ.

Once everyone finished grocery shopping, we got a ride back to the Airbnb with Al. And not long after we got inside it began to pour like crazy outside. It even hailed for a while! Everyone got comfortable back at the Airbnb and put on another movie. We all sat on the couch, talked, and enjoyed the show. I even got some editing done while we all hung out. Then just before 3PM I got a notification that we could go and check in at the room down the road. There was a break in the rain which felt like the perfect opportunity. I just wanted to drop everything off before the weather started up again. Then we would probably come back to the Airbnb to hang out with the gang later on.

The hippie shop in Pine was adorable and really fun to walk around. They even gave you these cute reusable bags with any purchase.

According to recent reports, the place that I booked for the night was called the Strawberry Inn, and it was really adorable. The location had a bunch of tiny home style rentals which were perfect for us. Plus, I was even able to book a room that had its own private hot tub. The idea of soaking in a hot tub while it rained sounded amazing. The room was perfect for the two of us and had everything that we could need. We got comfortable there and I decided to get some of my electronics charged. Then I went through my food bag to access how much more food I might need for this next stretch. I had even seen online that there was a Walmart nearby which would deliver. So that was going to be my strategy to get the rest of my resupply goodies at some point.

The big group of hikers hanging out outside of the hippie store in Pine.

Sources indicate that not long after we checked into the room, we were already hungry again. Luckily this location was right around the corner from the couple of different restaurants in town. At this point it was raining lightly but it wasn’t too terrible. So, we just carried our umbrellas and walked the short ways down the road to the bar and grill that was open. When we walked inside there was absolutely no indication that the place served food. The bar was full of guests, but nobody was eating. But they did indeed sell hot food! I wound up getting a chicken sandwich with a side of fried cheese curds. Those are really delicious. I also got a Dr. Pepper, but it had a really weird flavor likely due to coming from the bar soda gun. It was the strangest tasting Dr. Pepper that I’d ever had.

A chicken sandwich with a side of fried cheese curds!

In a recent development, slide and I hung out there for a bit and enjoyed our food. Then retreated back to the Strawberry Inn to relax for a while. I got some more editing done and Slide went through his photos. Then later on we decided to walk back over to the Airbnb to hang out with all of the other hikers. They were still watching yet another movie when we arrived. Truly though, what else is there to do in this town? We joined them for another one and wound up hanging out until sometime after 9PM.

One of the only joints open in the town of Strawberry.

Eventually we decided to walk back down the road to our room for the night. There is actually a breakfast place right next to the Inn which is going to be open tomorrow morning. It was closed today and the menu looks really good, so I’m excited to try that out tomorrow. We’re going to be taking our second zero day in a row tomorrow to wait out worse weather. Apparently, the rain is supposed to be much worse tomorrow than it was today, and more than an inch and a half of rain is expected over the course of the day. I’m looking forward to another day of rest and having some more time to get my writing and video editing done before we hit the trail once more.

If you enjoyed this blog and would like to support my hike by buying me a soda or a snack along the way, there is a “Tip the Author” button below! It links directly to my Venmo. Any and all support is incredibly appreciated!

The adorable tiny home at the Strawberry Inn that we’ll be staying in the next 2 nights.

Lucky Skier Survives Night in Crevasse With Two Broken Legs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border.
  • Industry observers note that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • Recent findings suggest that according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

Industry observers note that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

Recent findings suggest that according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

The following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

“He was really lucky,” noted Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

It has been revealed that by the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

#9410. Double Zero Days During More Arizona Trail Rain & Flash Flooding

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2001 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Double Zero Days During More Arizona Trail Rain & Flash Flooding

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this morning I actually slept in pretty late at our room in Strawberry.
  • Grabbing breakfast from the farm stand place in Strawberry.
  • Industry observers note that when we got over there a handful of hikers was hanging out and ordering some more food.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this morning I actually slept in pretty late at our room in Strawberry. It was nice knowing that there was no pressure to go anywhere or do anything. My only goals for the day are to get some editing done, eat a bunch of food, and resupply for this next stretch of trail. By the time that I did finally get up, Slide was very ready to eat. So, we decided to get our rain gear on and walk down the road to the breakfast farm stand right by the Strawberry Inn. I checked the hiker group chat and saw that a group of hikers from the Airbnb had walked over there and was hiding out from the rain in some kind of a shed. The place pretty much only has outdoor seating, but apparently the staff indicated the hikers where they could hide out and eat at the same time.

Grabbing breakfast from the farm stand place in Strawberry.

Industry observers note that when we got over there a handful of hikers was hanging out and ordering some more food. We got in line and ordered some stuff to take back and eat at our room, since it was right down the road. Everyone else finished up and wound up going back to their Airbnb to hang out. I figure we’ll head over there at some point today. But I also have a mountain of editing to get done, and it will definitely be easier to do it somewhere quiet. My eyes were way bigger than my stomach this morning, so I wound up ordering two things. The first was a lemon ricotta pancake, which sounded absolutely divine. And I also got a breakfast burrito to eat later on, just in case. On trail I always feel like I order way too much food or not nearly enough. Which is likely why I usually wind up ordering way too much.

The farm stand breakfast spot in Strawberry, AZ served one of the most incredible pancakes that I’d ever had.

We took the food to go and brought it back to the Strawberry Inn to eat and relax. And that lemon ricotta pancake was one of the best things that I’d ever had. I love ricotta but have never had it in a pancake before! Prior to getting on trail I was cooking a lot at home and making a ton of homemade pizza. Oftentimes I would top it with ricotta because it is so delicious. But this just opened my eyes to a whole latest use for the stuff. I didn’t wind up eating everything right away but figured I’d just graze on it for the next couple of hours.

In a recent development, after I ate, I decided to get right into business and start doing some writing and video editing. I also had an exciting call with a brand that I’ve worked with in the past and am going to be working with next year. My intends for 2027 are finally starting to come together and I’m really excited to be able to share it with you all eventually. The tiny home that we were staying in had a separate room which was pretty much the size of a walk-in closet. That was the perfect place to do some audio recordings and get certain work done for a while. Once all of that was done, I could get the rest of the work done more comfortably, while also watching a little bit of TV.

Industry observers note that in the afternoon I also had to place a Walmart delivery order to the inn. I had a lot of food, but definitely not enough to be comfortable for the next 71 miles. Our blueprint is to hike out of town and continue 71 miles to the next highway crossing, where we can go into the larger town of Payson. That will be about 3 days of hiking including the day out of town, and I’ve had a big appetite lately. It also sounded nice to get some drinks and snacks to enjoy this evening while we were at it. Before I placed the order, I messaged the hiker group chat to see if anyone needed anything random. Hikers always do! And sure, enough one hiker needed some sunblock and things like that. Which was easy enough to add on to the order. Plus, we’re going to be getting a ride back to trail tomorrow with a few of these hikers, so we’ll be seeing them.

Figuring out that you can do things in small towns such as place an online food order to be delivered is certainly a thru hiking hack. I had never even thought about doing anything like that prior to hiking the CYTC last year. Time was my most valuable resource and I was willing to do a lot to save it when I could. Oftentimes you’ll spend an hour walking to a store in town, resupplying, and then perhaps another hour walking back to the room. Some trail towns are spread out with miles between all of the essential locations. Oftentimes stores like Walmart won’t even charge a delivery fee for orders if you spend over a certain amount. Today I’m grateful to be able to do this and not have to hitch into the town of Pine to go back to the grocery store. Then hitch back once we’re finished.

In a recent development, while the Walmart order got delivered, I got a bunch more editing work done. I’ve also been sending a lot of emails and setting prepares into motion for my upcoming hike next year. It feels a bit like Deja vu, honestly. When I was hiking the CDT in 2024, I did the bulk of all of my planning for the following years border to border CYTC hike. There are so many logistics involved in a hike like that. Plus, you need a lot of gear! I remember dedicating serious time in towns to do video editing and also all of that coordinating back then on the CDT. Then when I finished up the hike I went home and had about 6 weeks to finish all of the planning and work as much as I could to save up money for the endeavor. I guess this is just the season for it. But this all feels very familiar.

This wound up being the perfect space to spend a couple of days off in town. I got most of my work done in that little room by the couch. And there is another bed on the other side of that wall.

Recent findings suggest that eventually our Walmart order got delivered, but not without minor concern. The driver had some trouble finding the place, which I was expecting. The address for our location was pretty confusing. But then after the groceries were delivered, I noticed an item that we hadn’t ordered. Then I realized we were missing a few things that we had ordered. Luckily, they were all drinks, so it wasn’t anything essential to us getting back out on trail. But they were sugary drinks that I was excited to enjoy. There isn’t any kind of a store or gas station in Strawberry, which is really the only thing that this town is missing. My favorite thing to do in town is to buy a bunch of different beverages and drink them all over the course of the day. Typically, on a double zero such as this, I would probably have bought a small case of soda or something like that. Liquid calories are my secret to not losing too much weight on trail.

By now the day was already starting to wrap up. Zero days on trail have such a miraculous way of slipping right through your fingers. It happens every single time without a doubt. At least I did get a lot of “work” done today and I also felt like I relaxed a lot. There really isn’t anywhere to go in this town, so there was no reason to be anywhere except for the room all day. A little after 5PM we started figuring out what to do for dinner. Everyone at the Airbnb had gotten so many groceries that they were just going to be staying in and trying to eat through everything. I wasn’t starving at this point, but I knew that later on I would be. Over the course of the day, I ate the rest of my lemon ricotta pancake and the whole breakfast burrito. That little farm stand in Strawberry was fantastic.

Sources indicate that surprisingly our options for dinner this evening were not limited. There were actually a few places open in town tonight because it was later in the week. One place sold empanadas, but they actually did wind up closing right before we were ordering food. Then there was also a steakhouse and an Italian restaurant. We wound up getting a massive white sauce pizza to split for dinner and were able to just walk down the road and pick it up. It was hardly raining at this point, though it had rained heavily for most of the day. It was pretty nice out when we walked to grab the pizza. The moon is incredibly full right now which is exciting moving into this next section of trail. I love night hiking when the moon is full.

Recent findings suggest that once we picked up the pizza we retreated back to the room for the rest of the night. The gang was just over at the Airbnb watching a movie. And while it would have been nice to hang out with everyone, I wasn’t in the mood to walk another mile just to watch a movie somewhere when I could just stay in bed and watch a movie there. It was too easy. The pizza was delicious and just what I needed. After we ate, I was contemplating going in the hot tub again. I went in this morning after breakfast and it was wonderful. But I think that going in first thing tomorrow will be even better. After eating I just relaxed for the rest of the night. I got a little bit more writing done and we watched TV for a while. Then I did my stretching routine and laid up on my phone for longer than I should have before finally calling it a night.

Sources indicate that if you enjoyed this blog and would like to support my hike by buying me a soda or a snack along the way, there is a “Tip the Author” button below! It links directly to my Venmo. Any and all support is incredibly appreciated!

I’m a thru hiker who has hiked 23,000+ miles in the last few years. In 2025 I became the 1st known woman to hike the “Border to Border” Calendar Year Triple Crown & complete over 10,000 miles of hiking in 1 year. In 2023 I became the 2nd known woman to hike the Eastern Continental Trail from Key West, Florida to Newfoundland Canada. I completed my Double Triple Crown between 2022-2025.

Weekend Warm-Up: Behind the Climb

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (436 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre.
  • As the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams.
  • The Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

As the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

The Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Industry observers note that hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

According to recent reports, interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

Ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed initiative.

It has been revealed that despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

Industry observers note that keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

At the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.
