#9403. Breaking: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1700 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1700 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Gribbin released his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • The journey has not gone according to proposal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin released his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to proposal. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

In a recent development, while he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Industry observers note that given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid plans. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

In a recent development, but this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

According to recent reports, for most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

In a recent development, northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and blueprint ahead.

The route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line shows the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

It has been revealed that I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with new designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

In a recent development, food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

According to recent reports, the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

Sources indicate that we have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Sources indicate that successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

According to recent reports, the huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

In a recent development, I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

You have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

According to recent reports, we were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

Industry observers note that there is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Sources indicate that back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

University changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

The decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

Industry observers note that the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

You can follow the expedition here.

Business & Policy ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Conservation Groups Warn Senate Bill Could Put Bears Ears, Boundary Waters and More at Risk

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A permitting reform bill presently before the US Senate would “effectively lock in project approvals that irrevocably open up recreation landscapes to development, including places like Bears Ears or the Boundary Waters,” states outdoor recreation advocacy group Outdoor Alliance.
  • Industry observers note that the Senate is currently voting on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), which is co-sponsored by Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Mike Lee (R-UT), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI).
  • Proponents argue the bill would lower energy costs, provide more regulatory certainty for developers, and facilitate future clean energy projects, but critics say it would weaken environmental protections and curtail public input.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A permitting reform bill presently before the US Senate would “effectively lock in project approvals that irrevocably open up recreation landscapes to development, including places like Bears Ears or the Boundary Waters,” states outdoor recreation advocacy group Outdoor Alliance.

Industry observers note that the Senate is currently voting on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), which is co-sponsored by Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Mike Lee (R-UT), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI). The bill’s aim is to speed up energy and infrastructure projects by streamlining the permitting process.

Proponents argue the bill would lower energy costs, provide more regulatory certainty for developers, and facilitate future clean energy projects, but critics say it would weaken environmental protections and curtail public input.

Bears Ears National Monument. Photo via Bureau of Land Management.

Sources indicate that the bill would narrow or change several existing environmental review and permitting requirements under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Clean Water Act, and Endangered Species Act. Crucially, outdoor recreation groups like Outdoor Alliance also warn that provisions designed to create “project certainty” for developers would make it difficult or impossible for future administrations to reconsider or modify permits.

The Center for Western Priorities, in partnership with Earthworks, has identified dozens of public-land landscapes that could be affected by the legislation, including Bears Ears National Monument, the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, and Tongass National Forest. The map highlights areas where existing or proposed mining, drilling, logging, and infrastructure projects could benefit from the bill’s provisions protecting federal development approvals from future reversal.

More than 110 mining claims have been filed in the Bears Ears area since the monument’s boundaries were shrunk, for instance. “Any mining looks approved by this administration would be nearly impossible to revoke, even if the monuments are restored,” the Center for Western Priorities writes.

Industry observers note that if BAAJA passes in the Senate, it will go back to the House of Representatives. Conservation groups are urging the public to express their support for public-lands integrity to lawmakers. Outdoor Alliance created an Action Alert to make it easy to contact members of Congress.

Featured image: Bears Ears National Monument. Photo via Bureau of Land Management.

#9394. Industry News: No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

Industry News: No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (386 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
  • “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • Industry observers note that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is quickly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

“We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

Industry observers note that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

Recent findings suggest that on the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

Industry observers note that once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

#9390. PCT Weeks 21 & 22: Aftermath

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3737 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

PCT Weeks 21 & 22: Aftermath

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was nice to be in a newly introduced town.
  • It has been revealed that we meandered along the river, and then the streets of the main part of town, which grew increasingly busy as the day went on.
  • According to recent reports, at the second brewery we went to, we instantly spotted a table of dirtbags.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was nice to be in a newly introduced town. Leavenworth is modeled on a Bavarian village, so I woke up knowing there’d be plenty to check out today. We walked into town to grab breakfast at a cafe that served expensive but delicious waffles, before venturing out to see the sights. It was a Saturday, and with Oktoberfest starting today and a marathon on tomorrow, the town seemed to buzz with a low thrum of energy.

It has been revealed that we meandered along the river, and then the streets of the main part of town, which grew increasingly busy as the day went on. We had bratwursts for lunch, and were dismayed when we jumped online and found out that Oktoberfest tickets had sold out. A little dejected, we headed back to the KOA for an afternoon rest. Well, I rested. Sass planned a little DIY Oktoberfest featuring stops at the breweries in town. In the early evening we headed into town to get started. We were still dressed in our trail clothes, so we stuck out like sore thumbs – as soon as we arrived in town we were picked out by locals as PCT hikers. They seemed pretty excited to see us, maybe because most hikers hadn’t made it to Leavenworth this year thanks to the wildfire trail closures.

According to recent reports, at the second brewery we went to, we instantly spotted a table of dirtbags. As we waited in line to order, we discussed in hushed tones whether they were thru-hikers or not. Drinks in hand, we walked past their table and discovered they were looking at us with the same curious eyes. Then I recognised a hiker I’d last seen in Major Bear, and all of a sudden we were sitting with them, exchanging news. This has been one of the best parts of trail life: being instant friends with other hikers. They were just finishing their drinks before heading into Oktoberfest. My FOMO was real.

Industry observers note that once they’d gone, and Sass and I had finished our drinks, we decided to at least go and ask if there was a walk-up ticket. And we were in luck! Soon we had cleared security and were on the hunt for our next drink. We paused by one stage where a stein-holding competition was in full swing. The winner really went for it – not satisfied with outlasting his competition, he held that thing up for minutes longer, clearly testing himself. Then we checked out a tent where live music was playing, where we found our friends from earlier and were swiftly invited to join them. It was a fun evening of exchanging more trail news, people watching, and singing along to Bavarianised songs. It felt very appropriate that one of them was ‘I’m Gonna Be (500 Miles)’ by the Proclaimers – basically the unofficial anthem of thru-hikers everywhere.

It has been revealed that sass and I had planned to thru-hike the Enchantments Traverse today, but when we woke up we were feeling the consequences of Oktoberfest. So we decided to postpone until tomorrow, instead. We were in no rush; we were planning to meet Catch in Bend in another week or so, and had plenty of time to kill. Plus, the PCT rate at the KOA was easily the cheapest accommodation we were going to find anywhere.

It has been revealed that we spent the morning crawling through coffee shops, then headed to the library to research hire cars to get us down to Bend in a couple of days. Then lunch, and back to the KOA for a few hours of rest before grabbing dinner and turning in early, ready for tomorrow’s hike.

📍 Enchantments Traverse | 🥾 35.65 km | ⛰️ +2,392m / -1,733m.

It has been revealed that we were awake bright and early, heading into town to pick up a coffee and then trying to hitch up to either of the trailheads for the Enchantments Traverse. Bizarrely, we got a lift with someone we knew! It was a couple we’d run into a couple of times on trail, and who’d been at the terminus with us. They’d been in town last night with friends, but had flights to catch later today so they could only drive us to the trailhead closest to town. Fine by us!

The trail started easily as we climbed well-maintained switchbacks. We made excellent time, and were confident we’d be done with the trail sooner than we’d planned, with plenty of daylight left to get a hitch back to town.

How wrong we were. After passing our first few lakes the trail began to enter tougher territory. Soon we were clambering over boulders, and in a couple of spots we lost the trail for a few minutes, but managed to find our way back. It got steeper and steeper. At the top of every climb I thought: this must be the top of the pass. Wrong. Every time.

It has been revealed that at least, once the toughest bit of climbing and navigating was out of the way, the scenery was sublime. The larches were in full, golden splendour, and the clear alpine lakes were glimmering in the sunlight. There wasn’t a cloud in the sky.

Sources indicate that sass cracked his head on a tree and ended up with a pretty decent open wound. Hikers streamed past in the other direction, telling us that Aasgard Pass had been pretty hectic. We brushed them off; we’d just done the PCT, how hard could it be?

According to recent reports, bloody hard, it turns out. There was clearly a reason most people hiked this trail in the opposite direction to us. Aasgard was a steep slope covered in both boulders and loose scree. It was a nightmare to downclimb. It took us at least two hours to get down to Colchuck Lake as we moved slowly, keeping our bodyweight low and trying not to twist an ankle or go sliding with the scree. About a quarter of the way down Sass realised that he’d lost his phone. How frustrating, especially since he had no idea where, and we hadn’t exactly been following a trail since it didn’t really exist amongst the rocks. The chances of finding it were slim. Daylight was fading, too; we didn’t have our overnight gear with us, so had no choice but to keep moving. I suggested we could come back tomorrow to look for it, but he noted there was no way he was climbing back up this heinous pass. He just hoped his terminus photos had uploaded to the cloud.

Recent findings suggest that we finally finished the pass and I was ready to rip out the final miles past the lake and down to the trailhead. Only the terrain remained rocky and difficult, and progress was much slower than I’d have liked. We ended up hiking for an hour in the dark, hoping against hope that this wouldn’t stop us from getting a hitch at the trailhead. We were glad to see that the carpark was still pretty much full when we arrived. Surely someone would come by soon. We were in luck: a car approached and Sass waved it down, giving the driver his sob story about his lost phone and head injury, and she immediately offered us a lift to town, which we gratefully accepted.

Industry observers note that today we were headed to Wenatchee, a larger town that had a Verizon store where Sass could get a replacement phone, and we could pick up a hire car. We’d originally planned to head to Mount Rainier and hike the open sections of the Wonderland Trail, but yesterday’s hike had beaten us to a pulp. So now we’d switched intends and were just going to grab the car for a day so we could get to Bend.

Recent findings suggest that sass had no trouble getting a new phone – and his terminus photos had made it to the cloud! – but the hire car was a different story. Neither of us had credit cards, and none of the hire places in town would rent to us without one. We spent several hours trying to figure out a new blueprint. Eventually, we found a place in Seattle that would let us hire with a debit card. So all we had to do was get to Seattle. We decided the easiest way would be to get the bus back to Leavenworth tomorrow, and hitch from there, since the locals are pretty used to PCT hikers.

Sources indicate that we were up in the dark to catch an early bus to Leavenworth. There, we grabbed a coffee and then headed up to the roundabout on the western side of town to try and hitch. We got a ride up to Stevens Pass pretty quickly, but then we were stuck there with our thumbs out for a long while. Eventually I headed up to the cafe to grab some cardboard and make a hitching sign; but while I was there Sass managed to score us a lift and we were on our way to Seattle.

Our hitch dropped us at a Costco on the outskirts, and from there we took an uber to the car hire place. As we drove along the busy highways I could feel myself growing a little sad. I didn’t like being back in this kind of civilisation. It was too much.

We picked up the car and, too scared to attempt driving on the wrong side of the road, I forced Sass to drive us the 6 hours to Bend. And as I doomscrolled in the passenger seat, I came across a post in the Enchantments hiking Facebook group: someone had found Sass’s phone! What were the chances? I put them in touch, then sat back and enjoyed the views of the mountains we’d hiked by only a couple of weeks ago.

Industry observers note that the days we spent in Bend were much the same. Our mornings were spent in one coffee shop or another, catching up on journal entries, going through photos, and doomscrolling. We’d head back to the motel for a supermarket lunch. We’d discovered the Bend Ale Trail app, and in the afternoons we made out our mission to visit as many as we reasonably could. When we grew tired, we headed back to the motel and turned on the tv, catching up on all the releases we’d missed while on trail.

Catch arrived in the evening of Day 150. He’d shaved and changed his clothes, and I hardly recognised him. We spent a good hour catching up on what we’d each been up to for the last week or so, then plotted our moves for this final section up to Government Camp and headed to bed early, eager to be getting back on trail.

📍 Mile 2,025.6 | 🥾 37.89 km | ⛰️ +1,293m / -1,037m.

I was not excited about going back to trail today. It was mostly because of the weather. The whole time Sass and I had been waiting around in Bend, the weather had been perfect – up to 27 degrees Celcius. But now, we were walking into a cold snap. Still, my desire to finish these miles won, and soon we were using a combination of Uber and hitching to get to the trailhead.

In a recent development, as we drove, the weather only deteriorated. As we passed through Sisters we were subjected to thick sleet. I decided that if conditions were like this at the trailhead, I’d hitch back to town and never mind the miles. But in the end the weather at the trailhead was ok, if a little windy.

Sources indicate that we’d already done the first ten miles previously, but with a light layer of snow on the ground the landscape looked entirely different. I’d been hoping to catch a better view of Three Fingered Jack, which had been largely obscured by smoke last time. But this time it was completely socked in by thick white clouds. We began to descend and were brutalised by the wind and lightly falling snow until we reentered treeline. We chatted from time to time, but it was so chilly that conversations didn’t last long. My lips wouldn’t move properly because of the cold. Our lunch break was only a quick pause to dig out our food, which we ate on the move to keep warm.

It has been revealed that I loved walking through the snow, it made everything so delicately beautiful. But I was too cold to bother trying to grab my phone out for photos. As the afternoon started to fade into evening I spotted the snowline on the trees, and began hoping that the campsite we were aiming for would be below it. And I was in luck. Although the spot wasn’t as tree protected as I’d have liked, it had to be warmer than camping in the snow.

📍 Mile 2,058.1 | 🥾 53.08 km | ⛰️ +1,446m / -1,894m.

Last night’s temperature hadn’t actually been that bad. The night between days 135 and 136 as we headed to the Canadian border had definitely been worse. It seemed like we were going to have much nicer weather today, too. I could already see glimpses of blue sky as we walked beneath the trees.

Mid-morning, the views started to open up and we caught great sights of Mount Jefferson, clouds dancing around its summit and eventually disappearing in the warm morning sun. Suddenly, I was very glad we’d decided to come back and do this section after all.

The climb up to the border of the Mount Hood Wilderness felt tough, though. I’d expected this section to be flat, as I remembered much of Oregon had been. Once we made it to the top, we scouted out some sun-warmed boulders where we paused briefly for lunch. Unfortunately, the sun wasn’t strong enough to keep us warm for long when we weren’t moving, so it wasn’t long before we were on trail again.

Sources indicate that we split up for the afternoon, which I enjoyed. I quite like having the trail to myself. And, at the back of the pack, it was really nice to know it was extremely unlikely that any other hikers would come along behind me. I was free of having to watch out for potential tailgaters.

There was a long burn zone, which was surprisingly rocky and boulder-y underfoot. Just as I was thinking it was a miracle I hadn’t tripped yet – I hadn’t even done one of the usual little toe stubs on a tiny rock – all of a sudden, I was falling. I struggled to regain my balance, but a bush was in the way of my feet and soon I had toppled completely. I just managed to save my face from smashing into a rock, but in the process I fell strangely on my wrist, pinning it underneath me. Ouch was an understatement. It was the same pain I’d felt when I rolled my ankle in NorCal, so I thought I’d probably sprained it. Suddenly, the solitude of the trail at this time of year didn’t seem so nice. I was thankful I had my Garmin inReach. Not that I needed it right now, but it definitely gave me some peace of mind.

Recent findings suggest that I struggled to my feet and continued on, trying my best to keep my wrist above my heart. It slowly began to swell to the size of a grape. Catch and Sass were ahead of me, but I hoped that at some stage they’d have stopped to let me catch up. I’d have liked their help getting my wrist compression wrapped. Worst case, we’d already agreed on a campsite, so I’d see them there.

The rest of the day’s miles were pretty tough. My wrist was searing with pain, and walking with it against my chest wasn’t natural or comfortable. Just after I passed the road into Olallie Lake Resort – which had closed for the season – a car drove past. I seriously considered backtracking to the road and trying to hitch literally anywhere, but in the end stubbornness to finish this section won out and I kept hiking.

I arrived at the campsite in the dark. Catch and Sass had been wondering where I was, so I filled them in, got my wrist strapped, and took a dose of ibuprofen. Then we sat together for a quick dinner before retreating to bed.

📍 Mile 2,089.7 | 🥾 51.59 km | ⛰️ +1,172m / -1,359m.

Recent findings suggest that my wrist was still painful in the morning, which I’d anticipated. At least today was our final day on trail and I could look forward to sleeping indoors tonight. Breaking camp took me longer than usual, and I had to ask the guys to help stuff my tent into my pack so I could close it.

Sources indicate that today’s trail was nothing particularly special. We stayed beneath the canopy for pretty much the entire day, so the audiobooks came back out as I plodded along. It was extraordinarily flat, though: I could see now why this section was popular for the 24 hour challenge. I tried not to take too many breaks, eager to be done with trail ASAP. And I ended up walking the last couple of miles at dusk, catching a couple of gorgeous glimpses of a rosy Mount Hood through the trees as I approached the trailhead where Catch had left his car.

It has been revealed that it was such a nice change to finish the day with a car waiting at the trailhead. We threw our packs in the back and drove to Government Camp, where we had enough service to search for an Airbnb. In the car, I realised I was properly sick. Sass had gotten a little sick on our last day in Bend, and I’d felt the usual warning sign scratchiness of a sore throat on trail. But it was only once I sat in that car, knowing we were done, that I felt the full force of it. I let the guys take the reins on booking the Airbnb, and soon we were inside, cosy and warm. We hadn’t bothered resupplying – the general store was already closed for the day when we arrived, and we didn’t want to drive further afield – so dinner was trail food. Sass handed me a NyQuil, saying as he did so that they never made him drowsy. But within 20 minutes of starting a movie, I was struggling to keep my eyes open, and had to retreat to bed early.

In a recent development, all three of us were sick as we rotted in front of the tv at our Airbnb for three nights. Although trail was really over now, I don’t think any of us had the energy to actually process it. It was kind of nice to have a good reason not to have to move from the couch, too. We spent our time watching a lot of endurance sports documentaries, venturing into Mount Hood Village only to resupply, and later into Government Camp for the sole purpose of grabbing another of the massive donuts from the Huckleberry Inn. Although on the way we also popped our head into the visitor centre and museum, which ended up having some pretty cool exhibits.

It has been revealed that on our last morning together Catch kindly drove us to Portland, where we wandered around a used bookstore to pick up copies of our next book club reads, and then enjoyed a final coffee together. I hadn’t really planned what I was going to do next, and after thinking about it on the drive, I decided to book a flight back to Australia for the next day. I knew I wouldn’t enjoy spending time – or money – in cities on the West Coast after being in the backcountry for so long. So in the afternoon we said goodbye to Catch who was heading off to meet another friend, then Sass and I grabbed a quick dinner and stuffed our checked-luggage-only items into cardboard boxes, ready for our respective flights.

According to recent reports, the next morning Sass left early to catch his flight. Mine didn’t leave until 7.30pm, so I hung around the motel until checkout, then ventured into town. I didn’t enjoy it. The hustle and bustle was too much for me, especially on a busy weekend, so I soon made my way back to the motel, collected my pack from behind the counter, and headed to the airport early.

According to recent reports, the flight was about as good as any long-haul flight can be. I read a little, watched plenty of movies and tv demonstrates, and had a few decent naps. Then there was a 3.5 hour train, followed by a 2 hour drive home. It was only then that I realised how tired I was, and practically collapsed into bed.

A week passed, and I finally gave into my parents’ nagging and went to the GP about my wrist. She sent me for an x-ray, and I discovered I’d fractured it. Unbelievable. I’ve never broken a bone in my life – unless you count my little toe, which I don’t, really. Earlier on trail we’d all discussed what our worst ever injuries had been, and I hadn’t had any good stories to tell. Now, I do.

Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (328 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
  • A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • The impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

The impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He said climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

Industry News: Never-Say-Die Climbers Will Try Everest Again This Weekend

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (317 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.
  • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.
  • It has been revealed that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

It has been revealed that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

This means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” remarked Kondrashkin.

It has been revealed that the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

On their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

#9381. Te Araroa day 22: Auckland here we come!

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2214 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Te Araroa day 22: Auckland here we come!

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that most of us (me, Lindsay, Sinead, Annabel and Anica) got going at around 7am again, although this time with good reason as we were expecting a bit of a longer day and needed to make a tidal river crossing later.
  • Coffee obtained, it was going to be a good morning!
  • Unfortunately, the day started with a decent road walk of about 7km, which I don’t think any of us had quite registered was coming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

27.5km, Mangawhai trail host to Pakiri Paradise.

It has been revealed that most of us (me, Lindsay, Sinead, Annabel and Anica) got going at around 7am again, although this time with good reason as we were expecting a bit of a longer day and needed to make a tidal river crossing later. The place we were staying was run by people who had previously done TA and provided everything hikers could need, at the very reasonable price of $10 per night. It was a great place to stay, and we walked out of the gate practically right back onto trail. We had been talking about coffee, but didn’t think that anything would be open at that time. But luck was on our side! Literally 50 metres down the street there was a coffee and smoothie van. What a great start to the day. While I was at university I was very much fuelled by coffee, but since then I’ve mostly switched to decaf. But I have been enjoying drinking it again while I’ve been hiking – it gives me a great energy boost, which puts me in a good mood, and I think the negative side effects I’ve experienced previously are reduced by having physical activity to funnel that energy into.

I found a friend when I went to pack away my tent.

Coffee obtained, it was going to be a good morning!

Unfortunately, the day started with a decent road walk of about 7km, which I don’t think any of us had quite registered was coming. Eventually we made it to the beach we would be walking along for the greater part of the day. The signage was familiar to me and I didn’t quite realise why until I registered that it was Auckland Council signage. We had made it to Auckland region! The Northland/Auckland boundary is just south of Mangawhai so that morning, we had completed the first region of Te Araroa. Northland is one of the longest (perhaps the longest?) regions on TA, owing to its long and thin geography. So this was a significant milestone. It was also probably the region I was least looking forward to, yet I loved it. Not every minute, of course, but distance had made my heart grow fonder and I was able to appreciate the beauty of the place with fresh eyes.

Industry observers note that the beach looked pleasingly short when we got onto it. That is, until I realised that the headland I could see was not the end of the beach section, but just a blip a few kilometres in. Still, the first section went pretty quickly and soon we were approaching the headland. There were hoards of surfers and foil board surfers, which looked pretty cool! There was also an interesting set up on the beach. Evidently a photoshoot was going on – a bed was set up, and a model posed on it in pajamas while a drone hovered and various involved people fluttered around. I’m sure the six dirty hikers walking through the background didn’t improve their shots!

The first part of the beach, looking towards Te Arai point.

Up on Te Arai Point, there were awesome views along the coast. The tracks weren’t super well-marked though, and the route was a bit un-intuitive. I was with Lindsay and Sinead at this point, and eventually we reached a wooded section that popped out on a road back to the beach. Just before the road we stumbled (almost literally) upon Zoe, who was taking a break in what she pointed out might be the last shade for a while. We plopped down to join her, and collectively decided that the rest of the beach necessitated podcasts. I realised I had forgotten to download more episodes when I last had wifi, and scrambled around for something to listen to. I tried an audiobook but I wasn’t really getting into it, and stopped to switch to music and try to find the specific song I had in my head that morning (u + me = <3 by Olivia Rodrigo, in case you were wondering). Tunes acquired, I set off again.

According to recent reports, this beach was actually perhaps the most annoying we have had to walk down so far. The tide was fully in at this point and the available area to walk on was soft, slopey, and narrow in places. There was one spot where the waves had created a bit of a cliff about 75cm tall, with very little space between the top of the cliff and the dunes behind. My feet were already wet from a stream crossing earlier, so I just decided to commit and walk in the water below the cliff. Apparently some of the others had taken their chances with the top of the cliff, with fairly unsuccessful results. It was a shame they were behind me, as the descriptions they gave of their falls were pretty amusing!

Walking over Te Arai point, with the surfers in the background.

Sinéad heading to the tidal crossing.

The other notable thing about the beach was the number of dead birds we came across. I really haven’t seen that many before. I hope it isn’t bird flu, which has recently arrived in NZ – perhaps it’s just something to do with the ocean currents that lots of dead stuff washes up there?

It has been revealed that at about 11:45 I was hungry. I was going to grab a snack and keep going, but realised I might as well stop for lunch. Who says lunch can’t happen before 12, anyway? I was hungry so I might as well eat properly. I enjoyed my wraps with fresh salad, although I kept dropping things that then got covered in sand. Annabel had told me about these sun-dried tomatoes that come without oil, and I had bought some in Mangawhai. They were great, 10/10 reccommend those. While I was lunching, the others all passed me. After a few more kilometres of walking, I came across everyone sat on the beach eating their (late) lunch. We were nearly at the tidal estuary, which the trail notes mentioned could be crossed 90 minutes either side of low tide. It was 2pm, and low tide wasn’t until nearly 5. But the others reckoned someone else had crossed outside of the reccommended window, and we decided to go and have a look.

Recent findings suggest that the butterflies were having a good dance in my stomach as we approached the estuary. I find rivers quite scary, especially when I don’t know how deep they’ll be. We went to the mouth, as that’s where the smaller streams on the beach had been shallowest. But the water here looked quite fast-flowing, so we went further up to a wider, slower bend. It was impossible to tell how deep it was, but at least we wouldn’t get swept away. Sinéad offered to be the guinea pig. She went up to her ankles, then her knees – and then she was basically across. No problem! We all followed without difficulty. Sometimes the trail notes really overstate the difficulty of a thing. I guess it can be deeper sometimes – but we crossed 3 hours before low tide with no bother, when the notes suggested 90 minutes. One of the most valuable pieces of advice I got about TA, which I tell to everyone, came from a couple of NOBO hikers that I picked up near Nelson Lakes last season. They remarked that there is a lot of scare-mongering from other hikers, but you have to see for yourself and not put too much stock in what everyone else is saying. And apparently the same goes for the trail notes, too!

The crossing was so fine! Zoe wading across with me, Lindsay, Annabel and Anica waiting. Photo by Sinéad.

Putting shoes and socks back on after the beach.

Sources indicate that we walked up the beach towards a holiday park. We were planning to go a bit further for the day but hoped they would sell us some cold drinks, and maybe fill some water bottles. It was a bit unclear where to go, but there was a man mowing the grass. ‘You lot look like an invading army!’ he called down to us. I suppose the six of us did look like we were plotting how to storm the castle! He invited us to come through the campground and rinse out our shoes and socks. After my sandpaper socks the other day, this was a very welcome invitation. He also said that the notes don’t give good advice about where to cross the river we had just been over. It’s much shallower inland, but the area is home to rare nesting birds, so DOC won’t allow the TA trust to tell people to cross further inland. Personally, I’m happy to wait a bit for the tides if it means not disturbing the birds. But I can see that it’s frustrating for the locals to see people being given less-good safety advice.

It has been revealed that after washing our feet, we all headed over to the shop where we bought ice creams and cold drinks, and checked out the next bit of the route. Everyone kept saying it was really steep, but for some reason I didn’t think it looked too bad on the map. Then I decided to look at a different map app, the one I normally use, and the contour lines looked way denser! I realised that the contours on the TA app are really light and narrow compared to the ones on the map I’m used to, so things don’t look as steep. I guess that could be helpful, in some ways.

It has been revealed that after a while, we headed off down the road. It was a fairly quiet road, and it wasn’t too long before we reached some track. The hill began immediately, and it was steep but not impossible. I ended up passing the others at the first flattish bit and continued on up. The views were pretty good and I felt happy about my fitness. I had a full 4 day resupply on my back but I found the hill ok, and I was able to keep plugging on without having to stop too often. Towards the top, there was a large fallen tree that I had to scramble over. Then I realised I was at the turn off for where we would be staying, and stopped to wait for the others. I watched them all clamber over the tree with varying levels of elegance. I would have taken photos but I didn’t want to walk back down the hill.

You can just see the others lower down the hill.

The house we were staying at was a couple of hundred metres along a side-track. Annabel and I got there first, and the couple came out and introduced themselves, and asked where we were from. Annabel is also from southern England, to which the guy responded that we were both ‘bloody Southerners’; he’s from Yorkshire! The rest of the group arrived and they showed us where we could pitch our tents. It wasn’t as luxurious as the previous night, but we had everything we needed. And, they showed us the view of Auckland city from their garden! This was the first time we had seen the city, and although it still looked very far away, it was cool to know we were getting closer. Everyone was planning to take some time off or visit friends in Auckland, and it’s also the first major city on the route. So it seems to have become a big milestone in everyone’s minds.

You can’t see it, but trust me when I say that the Auckland city skyline was visible in this view.

The weather was threatening rain so we pitched our tents, which were soaked from the morning dew still. I managed to snag a decent spot, but some of the others were less lucky and Annabel realised she had pitched her tent in a bit of a bog. Our hosts came out with a packet of scorched almonds, which was very nice of them! A little while later, Xavier showed up. He was at the campsite the previous night, but I didn’t end up speaking to him. Some of the others knew him from before, but I hadn’t met him so I took the chance to introduce myself. Then we carefully prepared dinner on the tables and chairs that kept sinking into the mud, and sat around talking for a while before calling it a night.

#9380. Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (599 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
  • Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
  • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My blueprint is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he stated.

According to recent reports, lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

Industry observers note that the Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch aims to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

It has been revealed that simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his plans while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

#9375. Te Araroa day 23: 500km in, have I found my trail legs yet?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2098 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Te Araroa day 23: 500km in, have I found my trail legs yet?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that most of the others left by 7am, but I was a bit slower and wasn’t ready until 7:15.
  • After a bit of up and down through cow fields, the track went into the bush and I caught up to Lindsay.
  • According to recent reports, at the top of the hill, I found Sinead and Xavier by a helipad.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

21km, Pakiri Paradise to Dome Cafe.

It has been revealed that most of the others left by 7am, but I was a bit slower and wasn’t ready until 7:15. But not to worry, as it’s a running joke that no matter how much later I leave, I’ll catch everyone up soon enough! I could see Annabel up ahead as I left, but the track went into some bushes and I didn’t see her anymore. The mud began pretty much straight out the gate, and at first I was able to avoid it reasonably easily. But it became apparent that I wouldn’t be able to go around it for much longer, so 15 minutes into the day I committed to the mud and put my feet straight in. The first steps are always the worst, and once your feet are already wet and muddy it doesn’t seem so bad anymore.

After a bit of up and down through cow fields, the track went into the bush and I caught up to Lindsay. This was interesting, as I hadn’t passed Annabel, and Annabel hadn’t passed Lindsay either. I figured I must have gone past without realising – maybe she was peeing in a bush or had gone the other way around a tree. Not too long after, there was a steep scramble up with some chains – the first (but not last) chains of TA! I don’t think I used them, but I always enjoy those steep scrambly bits. They use different muscles to the regular walking uphill ones, and it’s a mental puzzle as well as a physical challenge.

According to recent reports, at the top of the hill, I found Sinead and Xavier by a helipad. We had read about this helipad in the trail notes, and realised that it must be the same one that someone had posted in the TA Facebook group about using as a campsite one night. Unsurprisingly, that post got a number of comments telling him (more or less politely) that camping on a helipad is a pretty stupid thing to do! Fortunately we were not in need of a camping spot, and continued on. The track continued to go up and down, more or less steeply, more or less muddily, for a while.

What a great camp spot that would be.

Well good, because I sure was wearing some.

Sources indicate that eventually I started to hear traffic and surmised I must be getting close to the road. Shortly before the road, there was a steep, wet downhill section that was pretty boggy; and then, hilariously, a wooden bridge over a tiny stream at the bottom. This stream was barely a trickle, while the mud that came before it was at least ankle deep in places. What was the point of the bridge?! The random and pointless boardwalks continued for the last couple of hundred metres to the road. I appreciate the efforts to improve the track, but it really is futile to put a couple of metres of boardwalk in when they are preceded by several kilometres of mud.

At the road, I took a moment to enjoy my favourite hiker trash snack, mayonnaise on crackers. At this point Xavier appeared, and looked disturbed by my choice of topping. ‘Is that… just sauce?!’ My defence: plain crackers are boring, and I’m carrying the mayo for lunch anyway, so why not add more flavour and calories to my snack?

There was a short section of walking along the main road before I turned off onto a smaller one. On the map it was marked as a gravel road, but this was most definitely surfaced. Oh well. There were some decent views in places, and there was a house offering free filtered water. After not too long, I reached the next bit of track. I felt hopeful when I saw that it had steps, and gravel – maybe the next bit wouldn’tbe so muddy? The steps led up to a kauri dieback cleaning station, where I made a valiant attempt to get the mud off my shoes. It wasn’t very successful though – to make a real difference I would have needed running water. Then the track continued uphill on a gravel road/driveway for a bit. It was only 11am, but when I saw a nice grassy patch by the road I decided to stop for lunch. I wasn’t sure where the next flattish and dryish bit of ground would be in the upcoming muddy forest. I was able to have a nice lunch and dry my tent out, but it was getting pretty warm and by the time I got going again I was feeling full, sleepy and unmotivated.

The track went upwards for a bit more before turning off. I knew that this was where the 500km point was, and after missing the 300 and 400km markers I wanted to make sure I did something for this one. There wasn’t a suitable surface to draw on with my pole, so I gathered some small rocks from the road and wrote 500 with them. I took a couple of photos and headed back into the forest. The mud didn’t seem too bad at first, but became similar to the last bit of track. Up, down, up, down, mud, mud, more mud. Some of the downs were extraordinarily steep, too. Earlier in the day I had been able to enjoy the ridiculousness of slogging through mud for fun, but now my enthusiasm was wearing out. Most of the others had passed me when I was having lunch, but at the bottom of a particularly heinous descent I caught Sinead, who was standing in a stream. ‘We’re really close to the campsite now!’ she mentioned. The campsite she referred to was not where we planned to end the day, but a small one on the way at the end of this section of forest. Still, I was happy to hear we were close, and grabbed some water to filter when I got there. I knew there was a stream crossing just at the campsite, so I believed that Sinead was right and it was just around the corner. However after a bit more walking I checked my map and realised it wasn’t the stream crossing I was thinking of, and I was still about a kilometre away.

Eventually, we did arrive at the campsite. I could see Zoe sitting there with Xavier and one or two other people. Zoe set out early that morning as she was racing to meet some friends who were picking her up at the end of the day, and she must have been on a mission as I hadn’t seen her since the morning! She reckoned she got her trail legs all of a sudden – I would like to know if mine are on the way too, because this section was feeling hard!

Recent findings suggest that also there was Tim, who at first I didn’t recognise, but who I had met at the Ruakaka campsite on the day I arrived. He had been staying with friends and slack packing for a few days. In fact, we had followed him down the beach the previous day – I had seen the hiking pole marks in the sand and the figure in the distance, but not been able to work out who it was.

Recent findings suggest that lindsay and Anica soon showed up too, but there was no sign of Annabel. We were a bit worried about her, but there wasn’t much to do. At this point, it was about 2:30pm and we still had 7km to do to our intended stop at the Dome cafe. But the temptation to just stay at this perfectly pleasant spot was very strong. I knew I would be annoyed at myself if I stayed, so I washed my shoes and socks in the stream, reapplied my tape, had a snack, and got ready to continue. Someone had remarked that track conditions improved from this point, and I sure hoped that was the case otherwise it would be a rather late arrival into camp.

Finally some nice, dry track where I can actually appreciate my surroundings.

My first view of Rangitoto Island in the Auckland harbour.

Signs for improved track conditions sure seemed to be good. Across the road, the track went steeply up on a gravel forestry road. It was steep and hot, but at least not muddy. The gradient continued as the road turned into a track, but it was nowhere near as muddy as the previous sections. I was able to make good time, and when the track took a turn into some native bush, I was able to enjoy it. It was a nice bush track, although still of course rather hilly.

Sources indicate that A few kilometres from the end, I reached a trig point. Foolishly, I believed that it would be mostly downhill from here. Boy, was I wrong. There were still at least two substantial hills that just felt never ending. I caught up to Zoe at one point, and finally I came up to a viewpoint where there was a group of day hikers admiring the view, and Tim. I apologised for my smell and asked if it was far to the bottom. It had taken them 20 minutes to get up, which was music to my ears. The track from this point on was all gravelled, with steps. There was one small uphill, which felt massive to my tired legs. And finally, I was at the bottom. Zoe’s boyfriend was there, and introduced himself to me, but I was too tired to make intelligent conversation.

The track just after the trig was cool, especially when it was going downhill.

There is space for hikers to pitch tents kindly provided by the old Dome cafe, which is being turned into a house. They provide a small tent area, a sheltered kitchen area, and a hot shower! In a bath tub!! Unfortunately there was no curtain or anything around the shower, and it was a glass door out to the deck. So we had to take it in turns and make sure no one was there before heading round. In the past, I probably wouldn’t have been too keen on this arrangement, but I was so tired and desperate for a shower that I didn’t care. Then I was able to sit in a comfy chair and eat the mammoth dinner I had prepared for myself.

Annabel ended up appearing not too long after me, with Lindsay. It turned out she had got lost very early on when the track turned over a fence and she had continued straight on. She ended up not getting further than 1km on the track by 9:30, so it was very impressive that she had managed to catch up! We all agreed that this was one of the toughest days yet. The mud and the relentless up and down were physically challenging and a bit soul-crushing. Anica had actually gotten injured, and she planned to hitch the next day instead of walking.

Sources indicate that the floor lit up in the bathroom. Not quite to my taste, but it’s definitely something!

In a recent development, lindsay and I eat a well-deserved dinner. Photo by Sinéad.

The Dome cafe is just off SH1 north of Auckland, and I remember passing the DOC sign on the way up to Kaitaia. We could hear the road noise from where we were camped, and it was strange after a tough and remote-feeling day to be back so close to civilisation. I thought I would fall asleep promptly, but unfortunately the ground was not the flattest and I had managed to pitch my tent such that my head was downhill no matter which way I faced. In the end I shoved my rain jacket under my mat by my head, and was able to sleep.

#9368. Latest Update: TA Tales: Phase 4 – The Comeback

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (792 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: TA Tales: Phase 4 – The Comeback

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post is dedicated to my dear friend Ionatana.
  • Sources indicate that after completing the Auckland section of Te Araroa, Maya and I, headed to Hamilton.
  • So, our recovery continued along the Waikato River.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post is dedicated to my dear friend Ionatana. May God’s love, compassion, and mercy fill you, and your family up, then spill over with blessings.

Sources indicate that after completing the Auckland section of Te Araroa, Maya and I, headed to Hamilton. With a week of successful walking down, we felt another week of slack packing is maybe overly cautious, but (in my opinion) necessary. You can never be too careful when walking long distances. Taking care of injuries early, and not rushing through the recovery, is essential.

So, our recovery continued along the Waikato River. This is an established walkway for walkers, bikers, and boat racing watchers. Luckily for us, we managed to pick up this section of trail right as the Bridge 2 Bridge races were happening. Slalom skiers, inflatable speed boats, jet skis, and other raceable water craft wizzed past us as we meandered along the paved path.

It has been revealed that the trail, post river, takes you through Hamilton, and deposits you just west of town at the Taitua Arboretum. The weather was a bit stormy this week, so in true hiker fashion, we hunkered down, with our new British friends, at The Bank for the afternoon. We played cards, drank $4 pints, and enjoyed each other’s company.

Alice and Matt, our fresh favorite British couple.

Industry observers note that feeling fresh, rejuvenated, and healthy, Maya and I set off from the arboretum. Full packs, flexible walking blueprint, and high hopes, met by towering native trees, proved a great start to the next leg of our adventure.

The Karamu Walkway is 8.5 km of rolling hills with cool rocks and sheep. Seriously…sheep EVERYWHERE (25,000 to be exactish, according to our friendly trail host). We are just past the lambing season, so all the mama sheep are sheeping about with their lambs. Very cute, except for the fact that all sheep have a severe case of poopy butt, so just don’t look at their rear.

After our time with the sheep, we experienced our first hut. Picture the AMC’s High Mountain hut system, but a bit smaller, no “Croo”, and the huts are included in our trail pass. Mice…nope. Mattresses…yep. Awesome views and everyone staying there is super friendly…absolutely. The climb up and down the Pirongia Traverse was a true test for Maya’s knee, and she left that stretch feeling tired (of course, it was super muddy!), but energized from how great her legs felt. An overall win, and epic section.

Thank goodness for the board walks as you got closer to the hut.

In a recent development, sunset with Dr. Seuss tree from the hut deck.

Sources indicate that while the sections along the beaches, through farmland, and up and over mountains is why walkers walk, Te Araroa throws some lengthy road walks in there. You know, just to keep you grateful for the time spent not on the road. Walk it, hitch it, whatever. It’s your adventure. Maya and I do put our thumbs out when we can, but if we do end up walking it, we are well prepared with high visibility vests, custom made by Maya herself.

We are currently in Te Kūiti letting some weather pass and planning our next section which includes bike riding and canoe paddling. Sounds like a fun switch up giving our walking legs a rest, and our biking legs/paddling arms, some strength. Looking ahead appears to be pretty dang fun. Stay tuned to find out.

Sources indicate that P.S. I have been carrying a kite, and her maiden voyage was at Putaki Shelter. Her name is Putaki, Taki for short. I tried to fly her again at the Waitomo Top 10 Holiday Park, but the wind had a mind of its own that day. Let’s see how long she last.
